title: Maintain hygiene in food preparation, cooking and storage

lessons.title: Storing delivered food hygienically
lessons.html:
Why storage matters

Whether you work in a farm kitchen, an abattoir canteen, a packhouse staff kitchen or a farm stall, food that is stored badly can grow harmful bacteria, become contaminated by pests or chemicals, or simply spoil. In South Africa, food premises must comply with the hygiene regulations made under the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 (the general hygiene requirements for food premises, R638 of 2018), as well as your organisation's own procedures.

Receiving deliveries

  1. Check the delivery vehicle is clean and that chilled and frozen food arrived cold or frozen.
  2. Check temperatures of chilled and frozen goods with a clean probe thermometer and record them, using the limits your organisation sets.
  3. Check packaging: reject torn, swollen, leaking or dented cans and damaged packs.
  4. Check use-by and best-before dates.
  5. Check for signs of pests: droppings, gnawing, insects.
  6. Move chilled and frozen food into storage immediately; never leave it standing at room temperature.

Storage rules

  • Cold storage: keep fridges and freezers at the temperatures your organisation specifies; check and record daily.
  • Raw below ready-to-eat: store raw meat and poultry on the lowest shelves, below cooked and ready-to-eat food, so drips cannot contaminate it.
  • Cover and label all food, with the date opened or prepared.
  • FIFO: first in, first out. Put new stock behind old stock.
  • Dry stores: cool, dry, ventilated; food stored off the floor on shelves or pallets; opened packs in sealed containers.
  • Chemicals are stored separately from food, never above it.
  • Do not overload fridges; cold air must circulate.

lessons.title: Personal hygiene in food areas
lessons.html:
The food handler as a source of contamination

People carry bacteria on their hands, skin, hair, nose and mouth, and in the gut. Many food poisoning outbreaks are caused by food handlers. High standards of personal hygiene are therefore essential and are required by the regulations.

Personal hygiene standards

  • Clean protective clothing worn only in the food area: overall or apron, and a head covering that contains all hair.
  • Hand washing with soap and warm running water, drying with disposable towels, at these times: before starting work, after using the toilet, after handling raw meat, eggs or vegetables with soil, after touching face, hair or phone, after handling waste or cleaning chemicals, after breaks, and between tasks.
  • No jewellery except, where allowed, a plain band; no watches.
  • Nails short, clean and unpolished; no false nails.
  • No smoking, eating, chewing or spitting in food areas. Do not taste food with fingers or reuse a tasting spoon.
  • Cuts and sores covered with a brightly coloured waterproof dressing, and a glove where needed.

Illness reporting

Food handlers must report to their supervisor before starting work if they have diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, a sore throat with fever, skin infections, or discharge from eyes, ears or nose. The supervisor decides whether they must be excluded from food handling until recovered, according to organisational procedures and medical advice.

Why understanding matters

A food handler who understands why rules exist follows them even when unsupervised. For example, washing hands after handling raw meat prevents Salmonella or Campylobacter being transferred to salads that will not be cooked.

lessons.title: Waste disposal and keeping the area clean
lessons.html:
Why waste must be controlled

Food waste attracts flies, rats and cockroaches, and provides a place for bacteria to grow. Poorly managed waste can contaminate food, cause odours and break hygiene regulations and municipal by-laws.

Waste handling in food areas

  • Use bins with tight-fitting lids, preferably foot-operated, lined with bin bags.
  • Do not let bins overflow; empty them regularly and at the end of each shift.
  • Keep waste bins away from food preparation surfaces.
  • Wash hands after handling waste.
  • Clean and disinfect bins regularly, inside and out.

Outside waste areas

  • Store waste in a designated area away from the kitchen entrance, on a surface that can be cleaned.
  • Keep containers closed to keep out animals, birds and pests.
  • Arrange regular collection or approved disposal.

Separating waste

TypeHandling
Food scrapsClosed bins; composting or collection, as organisational policy allows
Used cooking oilCollect in containers for an approved recycler; never pour down drains
Recyclables (cardboard, cans, glass, plastic)Separate, clean and store for recycling
Chemical containersFollow label and organisational instructions; never reuse for food

Pest control

Report signs of pests immediately. Keep doors closed, fly screens in place and food covered. Pest control chemicals are applied only by trained or contracted people, away from food.

Key points

  • Check temperature, packaging and dates when receiving food, and store chilled food immediately.
  • Store raw meat below ready-to-eat food, label everything and use first in, first out.
  • Wash hands at all critical times and wear clean protective clothing.
  • Report illness before starting work.
  • Use lidded bins, empty them regularly and never pour oil down drains.
